headlines.text: Suppliers fear this company may struggle to pay the bills falling due in the next few months.
headlines.explanation: Liquidity, seen in the current ratio: Curanova's current assets cover its current liabilities only 0.7 times, against Medivale's 1.5 times. Below 1, short-term bills exceed short-term assets.

headlines.text: It keeps far more of every dollar of sales as profit after all its costs and taxes.
headlines.explanation: Profitability, seen in the net profit margin: Curanova keeps 16% of sales as net profit, Medivale only 9%.

headlines.text: Its medicines leave the warehouse and are restocked far more often than its rival's.
headlines.explanation: Efficiency, seen in inventory turnover: Medivale sells and replaces its stock 6 times a year, Curanova only 2.5 times.

headlines.text: Lenders worry whether this company's profits are enough to keep up with its interest bill.
headlines.explanation: Solvency, seen in interest coverage: Pillbridge's operating profit (EBIT) covers its interest only 1.3 times, against Medivale's 5 times.

headlines.text: It relies far less on borrowed money than its rival does.
headlines.explanation: Solvency, seen in the debt-equity ratio: Medivale has $0.5 of debt for every $1 of shareholders' funds, Pillbridge $2.4.

headlines.text: Hospitals take months to pay this company for the medicines they buy.
headlines.explanation: Efficiency, seen in the collection period: Pillbridge waits 95 days to collect from customers, Medivale 46 days.

headlines.text: Investors pay far more for each dollar of this company's earnings.
headlines.explanation: Market value, seen in the P/E ratio: investors pay 45 times earnings for Pillbridge's shares, 20 times for Medivale's.
